note: Written by Group 20 for this project. Sections T1-T5 restate the five provider schemes listed in the Kaggle dataset description; T6-T10 are common provider-level patterns described in general terms. Each section lists the features in our provider table that can show the pattern, and what the data cannot show.

chunks.title: Billing for services not provided
chunks.text: T1 Billing for services not provided (phantom billing). The provider submits claims for visits, admissions or procedures that never took place. Typical traces are claims for patients who had died, many claims per patient with no change in diagnosis, and unusually high claim counts relative to the number of attending physicians who could have delivered the care. In this dataset no claim is dated after a beneficiary's death, so the death check cannot fire; the usable signals are claims per beneficiary and claims per attending physician.

chunks.title: Duplicate submission of a claim
chunks.text: T2 Duplicate claims. The same service is billed twice, either by the same provider or by two providers, often with the same patient, date, diagnosis and amount. Signals are the share of a provider's claims that match another claim on patient, start date, first diagnosis code and amount, separately for matches within the provider and across providers.

chunks.title: Misrepresenting the service provided
chunks.text: T3 Misrepresented services. Claims describe a different service from the one delivered, for example a diagnosis chosen to justify a procedure. Traces include unusually many diagnosis codes per claim, many distinct admitting diagnoses relative to volume, and procedure codes on a high share of inpatient stays.

chunks.title: Upcoding to a more complex or expensive service
chunks.text: T4 Upcoding. The provider bills a more complex or costly service than the one performed, for example a higher-paying diagnosis-related group for an inpatient stay. Signals are reimbursement per claim and per beneficiary well above peers, a high maximum inpatient payment, long stays relative to peers, and a wide spread of diagnosis-related groups per inpatient claim.

chunks.title: Billing a non-covered service as a covered one
chunks.text: T5 Non-covered services billed as covered. A service the payer does not cover is coded as a covered one so that it is reimbursed. The claim lines in this dataset do not identify service coverage, so this scheme cannot be observed directly; at most it raises reimbursement per claim, which overlaps with T4.

chunks.title: High-volume billing operations
chunks.text: T6 High-volume billing. A provider files far more claims, and receives far more reimbursement, than peers of the same type. Volume alone is not evidence of fraud, because large hospitals legitimately bill more, so a volume flag should be compared against size-adjusted measures before escalation. Signals are total claims, total reimbursement, inpatient claim counts and the number of beneficiaries.

chunks.title: Excessive length of stay
chunks.text: T7 Excessive inpatient stays. Admissions are extended beyond clinical need to raise payment, or stays are billed for longer than they lasted. Signals are mean and maximum length of stay and the share of stays of ten days or more, compared with inpatient peers.

chunks.title: Physician concentration
chunks.text: T8 Physician concentration. A large share of a provider's claims carry one attending physician, or the same physician appears as attending and operating on most claims, which can indicate identifiers being reused rather than care being delivered by a team. Signals are the top attending physician's share of claims, claims per attending physician and the share of claims where attending and operating physician coincide.

chunks.title: Shared patients and referral rings
chunks.text: T9 Referral rings. Groups of providers share many of the same beneficiaries and refer them among each other, so that each provider bills for the same people. Signals are the number and weight of provider links through shared beneficiaries and the share of a provider's neighbours already flagged. Because large providers are linked to many others by chance, these signals must be read against provider size.

chunks.title: Patient mix inconsistent with billing
chunks.text: T10 Patient mix. The conditions and ages of a provider's patients do not match the intensity of what is billed, for example high inpatient payments for a relatively healthy population. Signals are the mean number of chronic conditions, the share of renal disease patients and beneficiaries' annual reimbursement, read together with reimbursement per claim. Patient-mix features can also penalise providers that legitimately treat sicker patients, so they should never decide a case alone.
